The FBI is reportedly investigating an identity theft case involving the sale of electronic scans of more than 153 million driver's licences on the dark web. The massive security breach also exposed other documents including medical cards and residency cards.

These driver's licences belong to individuals in the United States and Canada and are said to have been obtained by hacking into an identity verification services company……

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the cybercriminals' claims as true, as they were able to provide a scan of the site editor's own driver's licence, and other victims also confirmed that their scans were accurate.

A new identity theft service called Nexus has debuted on the dark web this week, selling electronic scans of more than 153 million driver's licences belonging to individuals in the United States and Canada. The operators behind Nexus claim that these licence images were obtained from an ongoing security breach at a "large identity verification company" whose clients include multiple Fortune 500 companies. KrebsOnSecurity has also learned that the FBI's New Orleans field office has today formally opened an investigation into the source of the images.

Reports indicate that the identity verification company appears to be a business headquartered in Louisiana. The criminals claim they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by the fact that they added nearly 400,000 new files within the past 24 hours.

There are indications that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by the car rental company Hertz. Reports point to a company headquartered in New Orleans as a potential source, and its client list includes Hertz, Target, FedEx, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. See the full report for details.

9to5Mac's take

It's almost ironic — if it weren't so serious — that criminals were able to hack into an identity verification service to obtain documents that can be used for identity theft. Unfortunately, such security breaches have become commonplace.

According to recent estimates, cyber fraud cost Americans close to US$150 billion last year, with the number of cyber scams continuing to rise sharply.
